compression.title: IPTC photo metadata tests
compression.lede: are the IPTC Photo Metadata Working Group's tests of what sharing sites and systems do to the metadata embedded in a photograph: upload, view, save, download, then check whether its Exif and IPTC fields survive (2013, 2016, 2019). The IPTC Photo Metadata Standard they test is a distinct object (2019 page; census record).

sentences.text: The IPTC photo metadata tests are the IPTC Photo Metadata Working Group's checks of what image-sharing sites and systems for sharing files and messages do to the metadata embedded in an uploaded photograph: the IPTC "checks about a dozen sites regularly: in 2013, in 2016 and now again in Spring 2019," each time against its own claim that "embedded metadata should not be removed" from shared images (IPTC, Social Media Sites Photo Metadata Test Results 2019), and the provenance census record names the series, gives its operator as the IPTC's Photo Metadata Working Group, and records that it both expresses and tests provenance (provenance census record).

Each test uploads an image whose embedded values are all known, "e.g. the latest Reference Image File," checks what the site displays, saves the image with the browser's Save As and downloads it through the system, and asks of each file whether "the embedded Exif and IPTC metadata (in the formats IIM and XMP) of the uploaded image" are "still embedded" (2019 page); the census record keeps the same operations as the transformations tested, embedded metadata inside the file as the carrier, and the site or system as the unit (provenance census record).

Four fields are checked on display, "Caption/description, Creator, Copyright Notice, Credit Line (= the 4Cs )" (2019 page), which the census record carries as the relations tested: creation, credit, rights and description (provenance census record).

The IPTC gives the series its origin: users "discovered that when they shared photos via social media sites or systems, their embedded metadata disappeared," and the Working Group "tested 15 social media sites in 2016 and 2013 to understand how image sharing, through upload and download, affects the integrity of embedded metadata" (IPTC, Photo Metadata Research).

The research is the IPTC's second activity beside the standard, "IPTC not only defines the standard for photo metadata, but also conducts research about how photo metadata is used and implemented" (Research page), and the IPTC's Photo Metadata page, the composition's first card, says so in the same terms and adds: "The removal of rights information as images are transferred is of particular concern" (IPTC, Photo Metadata).

The census record dates the series to 2013, 2016 and Spring 2019, with a software test published in August 2014, counts 15 sites in 2016 and 2013 and about a dozen in 2019, and was read on 2026-10-29 (provenance census record).

In the Spring 2019 tables Pexels, pixabay and Unsplash strip the metadata from saved and downloaded files, and on Flickr the "Embedded Creator" is "replaced by account owner" while saved files lose their XMP (2019 page).

Among the systems for sharing files and messages, Facebook keeps "A few rights related fields" in IIM and Exif and writes two IIM fields of its own, Twitter strips saved files, and Dropbox and OneDrive pass the original through while their previews save "with stripped off metadata"; Behance's saved files "keep the embedded metadata" (2019 page).

The census record keeps the same year and the same losses as its retention results: of eleven image-sharing sites, Pexels, pixabay and Unsplash stripping, Flickr replacing the creator with the account owner, Twitter stripping on Save As, Facebook keeping a few rights fields (provenance census record).

The research page reads the series as showing that some sites "remove embedded information like copyright notes, the name of the creator, the description and more, while others protect photographers’ data better," and that "it is not impossible to preserve metadata in a workflow"; its software study of August 2014 found rights fields in half of the programs tested, retrieval of embedded rights data in two out of three, and two programs that "didn’t support rights metadata at all" (Research page).

The norm the tests measure is the IPTC's own: its User Guide endorses the Embedded Metadata Manifesto, under which "Copyright management information metadata must never be removed from the files," removal being "forbidden by law in many countries," and its minimum set of fields "is not a permission to strip off metadata" (IPTC Photo Metadata User Guide, November 2025).

The same guide and the IPTC's Google Images FAQ place the loss also in the sites that host images: a site's "digital asset management system, content management system, image management system or content delivery network may be stripping out embedded metadata fields" (User Guide), the metadata "might be stripped from your images by some software on your site," a DAM, a CMS such as WordPress or Drupal, or a CDN such as Cloudflare (FAQ), and NeededApps' explainer holds that metadata is no "infallible form of copyright protection because it can be removed or modified" (NeededApps).

The archive reads the same loss at other carriers and stages: in-pixel metadata "survives screenshot, rehosting, filename change, metadata stripping, PDF embedding, and sidecar loss," so the archive's handwritten artifacts carry their metadata three times, "in the pixels + embedded (IPTC/XMP/C2PA) + external" (#1409), and the publication layer's provenance signals, C2PA manifests and structured metadata among them, "are stripped or rendered invisible long before they reach the training corpus. The body text is what survives" (#127).

The object the tests test is a distinct entity, the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard, which "sets the industry standard for administrative, descriptive, and copyright information about images" (IPTC, Photo Metadata): its properties are grouped "into Administrative, Descriptive and Rights-related properties" (Photo Metadata Standard 2025.1) in two schemas, IPTC Core and IPTC Extension, "built on the legacy of the original IPTC-IIM" (IPTC Photo Metadata Standard page), and the census record gives the object they bear on as "the photograph as a file: embedded Exif and IPTC metadata (IIM and XMP)" (provenance census record).

Its current release is 2025.1, "including … IPTC Core Metadata Schema 1.5 … IPTC Extension Metadata Schema 1.9" (specification, About the Standard), while the same specification heads its Extension section "IPTC Extension schema 1.8 specifications" (specification, contents and body).

Its genealogy runs from the IIM, "developed in the early 1990s by the International Press Telecommunications Council (IPTC) to expedite the international exchange of news" (Wikipedia, IPTC Information Interchange Model), whose image properties were embedded as the "IPTC header" (Wikipedia, International Press Telecommunications Council; Wikipedia, IIM), to XMP, which "has largely superseded IIM's file structure" (Wikipedia, IIM), the IPTC having worked "alongside Adobe" on an implementation that "employs Adobe’s XMP technology" (Standard page); Core fields embedded in both formats must have their values synchronised by the image software (User Guide).

The standard leaves the file and the camera to others: how its formats are stored inside image files is "defined by non-IPTC file format standards, such as JPEG/JFIF, TIFF, PNG and more" (Standard page), and the specification "does not include any technical metadata" (specification), the capture data NeededApps assigns to Exif while IPTC metadata "is commonly used to describe, organize and manage images" (NeededApps).

The IPTC calls it "the most widely used standard to describe photos, because of its universal acceptance among news agencies, photographers, photo agencies, libraries, museums, and other related industries" (Standard page), Wikipedia "by far IPTC's most widely used standard" for its "nearly universal acceptance among photographers" (Wikipedia, IIM), and its stated uses are "protecting images' copyright and licensing information online" and "managing digital assets" (IPTC, Photo Metadata).

Its operator, the International Press Telecommunications Council, is "a consortium of the world's major news agencies, other news providers and news industry vendors" that "acts as the global standards body of the news media" (Wikipedia, International Press Telecommunications Council), and its own conference video marks "20 years of IPTC Photo Metadata" (IPTC, YouTube, title only).

The 2025.1 release, announced by the Working Group on 27 November 2025, adds four properties "for AI-generated content", AI Prompt Information, AI Prompt Writer Name, AI System Used and AI System Version Used, the third defined as "The AI engine and/or the model name used to generate this image" (IPTC news; Standard page), beside the Data Mining property, a "Data mining prohibition or permission, optionally with constraints" (specification).

The User Guide gives their purpose, to tell AI-generated images from "regular" ones "to avoid re-training AI models on content that was already generated by a model," and recommends leaving Image Creator empty and setting Digital Source Type to trainedAlgorithmicMedia or compositeSynthetic (User Guide); the announcement records that writing the new properties into its example image "has rendered the C2PA metadata invalid" (IPTC news), and the census record marks the tests "NOT a test of C2PA credentials" (provenance census record).

The archive places this layer of the standard: "IPTC AI metadata" is "Layer 1 metadata", "Disclosure, not lineage", where artifact provenance "operates at the moment of artifact creation" and the dimensions of provenance are independent, each preserved or destroyed "regardless of the others" (#725), and against the reading of provenance as "a field, a tag, a manifest, a credential, separable from the object it documents," #725 holds that "To strip provenance is to change what the meaning *is*" (#725).

The archive uses the standard's vocabulary for its own artifacts: Digital Source Type declared as digital capture of a physical original is "the nonsynthetic claim made machine-readable inside the file," the archive's scaffold, "everything machine-readable around the ink," takes in IPTC/XMP/EXIF, and "C2PA, FADGI, and IPTC provenance vocabularies are the same insight arriving as standards" as the archive's substrate checksum (#1409).

Google reads the embedded fields: it "displays three IPTC photo metadata fields, wherever available," telling the viewer the creator, the copyright holder and the credit line (User Guide), a display "introduced by Google in September 2018" (IPTC Guidelines & Support), "Google extracts this information from photos in search results" (FAQ), and the IPTC's browser extension sends a web image to its GetPMD tool, "which will display all metadata embedded in the image file" (Chrome Web Store).

The archive records the same channel as established for extraction and open for composition: IPTC photo metadata "embedded in the file (travels with the image across pages)," "ESTABLISHED as extracted; composition role unknown," and "scaffold the pipeline provably reads" (#1409).

The census record holds the series historical, "the 2019 table is not a 2026 platform measurement," succeeded in method by the IPTC's Metawatch (2026), which it records as a part, with C2PA conformance its neighbour; it tags the series "NOT a current platform audit," leaves the 2016 and 2013 tables, the 2014 software study and the interoperability procedures unchecked, and kinds it a test series (provenance census record).

Its organizing question is asked of every entity alike: "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?" (provenance census record).
Wikipedia has no article on the tests, and none at the title IPTC Photo Metadata (Wikipedia, as fetched 2026-10-29).

At the bare name on Google's AI Overview the Capture Registry gives the innocent reading first, the standard explained "from the IPTC's own pages," and finds the standard held: "Core and Extension, IIM and XMP, the 2025.1 release and its AI properties are the IPTC's own," with the IPTC named, "no person; no identifier" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

It records that the record at the name is the tests and their 2019 losses, that "None of this is in the composition," which "composes the carrier and leaves out the measurement of its erasure," gives the search engines' reading of the data and "omits the loss," heads the 2025.1 properties "AI & Content Provenance" where the IPTC gives them as properties of AI-generated content, and cites no card of the record that landed the same day; it reads the capture as "the baseline for the name" and "the measurement of stripping" as "a second address" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

F15.quote: By defining this set of minimal metadata properties IPTC does not support any removal of existing metadata outside this set without the explicit permission of the copyright owner of the image. (In simple words: this is not a permission to strip off metadata and is not legal advice.)

F18.quote: Your site’s digital asset management system, content management system, image management system or content delivery network may be stripping out embedded metadata fields. Some systems do this with the best of intentions, thinking that it will save a few bytes of bandwidth, but stripping out metadata actually infringes on the copyright holders' rights and may even be illegal in some countries.
F18.source_label: IPTC — IPTC Photo Metadata User Guide
F18.locus: 'For developers and site administrators: how to ensure the fields are preserved in images on your site'

F33.quote: In that case, the metadata might be stripped from your images by some software on your site. In other cases your Content Management System (such as WordPress or Drupal) might strip off metadata. Or it could be a Content Delivery Network that you use, such as Cloudflare or Cloudinary.
F33.source_label: IPTC — Google Images and IPTC: Frequently Asked Questions

F31.quote: Metadata shouldn't be treated as an infallible form of copyright protection because it can be removed or modified, but it provides useful information that can travel with the image.

F19.quote: It may be important to distinguish AI-generated images from "regular" images: for example, to avoid re-training AI models on content that was already generated by a model, to understand which images can fall under copyright and which cannot (in some jurisdictions) and to avoid misinterpreting generated images as being real photos.

O725-02.quote: Artifact provenance (C2PA) verifies that *this file* was created by *this source* at *this time*. It is necessary but operates at the moment of artifact creation. … The three dimensions are cumulative and independent. Each can be preserved or destroyed regardless of the others.

F32.quote: IPTC maintains the technical standard that image creators can use to put their creator and copyright details inside image files. We call this “photo metadata”. Google extracts this information from photos in search results and displays it to help you find who owns the image.

F34.quote: IPTC's Photo Metadata Inspector tool lets you see embedded metadata in many image files. For eligible images, a context menu will appear when you right-click on the image. CAP-1-10.quote: Asked for IPTC photo metadata, the Overview explains the standard from the IPTC's own pages: what it holds, how it differs from camera data, how it has grown to describe images an AI system made, and the tools that read it.

CAP-1-01.quote: Core and Extension, IIM and XMP, the 2025.1 release and its AI properties are the IPTC's own (cards 2, 3 and 5).

CAP-1-09.quote: The IPTC named; no person; no identifier; the IPTC's own pages cited (eight of eleven cards).

CAP-1-02.quote: The census row at this name is the IPTC Photo Metadata Working Group's tests of what platforms do to embedded metadata: Pexels, pixabay and Unsplash stripped it from saved and downloaded files, Flickr replaced the embedded creator with the account owner (2019).

CAP-1-03.quote: None of this is in the composition. At the bare name the Overview composes the carrier and leaves out the measurement of its erasure.

CAP-1-06.quote: At the bare name the composition layer gives the standard at the grain of its own documentation and leaves the census row's object, the record of the standard's erasure in transit, unsaid.

CAP-1-04.quote: The composition says search engines read the data 'to display creator information and licensing attributes directly in search results', from IPTC's Google Images pages. The same organization's tests record that the data is often gone before any engine can read it; the composition gives the reading and omits the loss.

CAP-1-05.quote: 'AI & Content Provenance' is the composition's heading for the 2025.1 properties; the IPTC announcement (card 5, 27 November 2025) gives them as properties of AI-generated content.

CAP-1-08.quote: A baseline: the record landed on provenanceerasure.org the same day (commit 8a9f153) and no card cites it.

CAP-1-07.quote: The record keeps the tests as its unit; the capture is the baseline for the name, and shows that the measurement of stripping is a second address.
